summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since 1998 and are legal throughout the country. The statutory position offers little practical protection: there is no protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in Tajikistan's legislation, and a 2020 ECOM legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners identifies legal barriers and gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, documenting cases where the written law protects but practice does not.

Authorities maintain a register of LGBTIQ people, introduced by police in 2016 and described by Outright International as a 2017 government registry of "proven" LGBT persons. ILGA-Europe's annual review for 2024 reports that police lure LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvest their social-media contacts and extort money, with more than ten such cases recorded in Sughd province.

Raids conducted in 2022 and 2023 in several cities brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges. The IPHR report documents ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police. In 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people, involving arbitrary arrest by police, blackmail and extortion.

Forced or sham marriages are imposed on LGBT people, and police decline to intervene. The 2022 anti-discrimination law does not address discrimination on these grounds and only partially aligns with United Nations standards.

Access to care is a live concern: a 2024 ECOM study examines trans people's access to medical services, including HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy, across the wider region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing and guidance included for trans migrants.

For a visitor: there is no expression statute, but registry practices, police entrapment and the absence of any recourse make discovery dangerous. People who disclose their orientation or gender identity become targets of physical and psychological abuse, including abuse by police.
tangentialFactors:
The repressive context surrounding LGBT life in Tajikistan is documented well beyond the registry itself. Human Rights Watch reported that the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016, with opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule.

Reporting from 2013, fifteen years after decriminalisation, found very little tolerance in practice and described the community as one of the most closed in society, with those who disclose facing abuse from police as well as from the public. That evidence predates the 2016 registry and indicates a social climate that the formal legality of same-sex conduct has not altered.

The pattern is regional rather than unique to Tajikistan: ECOM's 2024 study of trans access to medical services covers the wider eastern Europe and central Asia area, and its 2020 legislative analysis is explicitly comparative, placing Tajikistan's legal barriers alongside those of neighbouring states.

ILGA-Europe's assessment that the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with United Nations standards sits alongside the IPHR finding that the same law fails to address discrimination, so the legislative instrument and its enforcement gap are reported independently by two sources.
localsOnly:
Tajik residents live under a police register of LGBTIQ people that has operated since 2016, with a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons recorded in 2017. Registration can be triggered by a fake meeting arranged by officers, and the contacts harvested from social-media accounts are used for extortion; more than ten such cases were documented in Sughd province during 2024.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2022 anti-discrimination law does not cover these grounds and only partially meets United Nations standards, so residents who are dismissed, refused service or assaulted have no legislative hook.

Forced and sham marriages are imposed on LGBT residents, with police inaction leaving families and spouses without a remedy. Arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion by police were the substance of 27 recorded human-rights violation cases against LGBT people in 2024.

Practical barriers to healthcare are documented for residents as well as visitors: the 2020 ECOM legislative analysis sets out legal gaps affecting gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, and the 2024 ECOM study addresses access to HIV prevention and treatment and to hormone replacement therapy, work in which a Tajikistan country coordinator participated.

Disclosure carries a documented cost. People whose orientation or gender identity becomes known face physical and psychological abuse, including abuse originating with police, and the community remains among the most closed in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 chapter on Tajikistan contains no material on transgender prisoners or prison housing. Its detention references concern opposition figures and deportees rather than the placement or conditions of trans detainees, so the treatment of trans people in Tajikistani custody is unresolved on this inventory and should not be inferred either way.

Legal gender recognition, including whether a trans visitor or resident can change identity documents or gender markers, is not addressed by any source in this inventory. That question remains unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for Tajikistan, including any document inspection that could disclose a traveller's trans status, are not covered by these sources and are unresolved.

The exact provisions of the 2022 anti-discrimination law are described only in general terms by the sources available; the specific articles, penalties and complaint mechanisms have not been verified.

Whether the police registry distinguishes trans people from lesbian, gay and bisexual registrants, and how many people it currently holds, is not stated in the inventory.
